stem: An analytics role in account B needs to read objects in an S3 bucket that account A owns. The role's identity-based policy in account B already allows s3:GetObject on the bucket's objects, but requests are still denied. Without sharing any long-term credentials, what should the data team in account A add?

choices.text: An SCP in account A's organization that allows the account B role to call s3:GetObject on the bucket
An AWS DataSync task that copies the bucket's objects into a bucket in account B
A bucket ACL that grants read access to account B's AWS account
A bucket policy that allows s3:GetObject on the bucket's objects for the account B role's ARN

rationale: For a request from one account to another, the requester needs an identity-based policy in its own account and the resource-based policy in the owning account must also allow it. The role already has the first half, so account A adds a bucket policy that names the role and allows s3:GetObject. An SCP never grants permissions; it only limits the maximum permissions of principals in member accounts. AWS DataSync copies data between locations; it does not grant the account B role permission to read the original bucket in account A, and the analytics role's identity-based policy already targets that original object, not a copy sitting in a different bucket. A bucket ACL granting READ to account B's AWS account is not the fix: on a bucket, READ allows the grantee only to list the objects (s3:ListBucket), not to read their data (s3:GetObject), so it would not satisfy this request even if it were the only problem; new S3 buckets also default to the Bucket owner enforced setting, which disables ACLs entirely and means AWS access-management policies, not ACLs, control access. A bucket policy is the supported way to scope resource-based access to one caller's ARN.
